title: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (5 of 7)
hook: whoever sees all beings in the self no longer shrinks from anyone
tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (6 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: renounce and enjoy, and the one who moves and does not move, far and near, inside all this and outside it. Did you check what was near? Day two hundred thirty-six.

A man on the train is talking to himself, loudly. A relative starts in on politics at dinner. A bad photo of your own face turns up. And something in the body pulls back, a small recoil, before a single thought has formed. Verses six and seven of the Isha are about that flinch. They say there's a way of seeing that makes it go away. Not by trying harder to be nice. By seeing differently.
screen: `THE FLINCH.` → `A SMALL RECOIL.` → `A WAY OF SEEING.`

segments.voice: Verse six: the one who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, does not shrink away from anything. The verb is vijugupsate: to recoil, to feel aversion, to shrink back in disgust. That's the flinch, named. And the cure isn't a rule. It's a seeing. If the same self is in you and in the man on the train, then pulling away from him is a bit like pulling away from your own hand. Verse seven goes further. For the one who sees oneness, ekatvam, what delusion is there, what sorrow? It's phrased as a question, the way verse one ended. Not no sorrow ever, but: where would sorrow get a grip? Then verse eight describes the one who pervades all this, and it's a lovely list. Bright. Bodiless. Without wound. Pure. Untouched by evil. The seer, the wise one, the one who is everywhere, self-existent, who has set things in order for all time. Notice how this connects to the week. On day one, all this is pervaded by the Lord. Here, you see the same in every being. Renouncing, on this reading, isn't only letting go of things. It's letting go of the wall between you and everyone else. And enjoying becomes something bigger: not just enjoying your coffee, but not having to flinch. You met this idea in the Gita too, where the sage sees the same in a scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and the one who eats dogs. The Isha puts it in two lines.
screen: `ALL BEINGS IN THE SELF.` · `NO LONGER SHRINKING BACK.` · `WHAT SORROW, FOR ONE WHO SEES ONENESS?` · `BRIGHT, BODILESS, PURE.` · then, large: `THE SELF IN ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Bring to mind someone you flinch from a little. Not the hardest person in your life; someone mildly difficult. Picture their face. Notice the small recoil in your body: the jaw, the shoulders. Breathe into it. Now try the verse, just as an experiment: the same life that's breathing in you is breathing in them. Keep their face in mind and see if the flinch softens, even slightly. If it doesn't, that's fine. You looked. The bell holds the time.
Renounce and enjoy. Verses six and seven: renounce the wall, see all beings in the self and the self in all beings, and stop shrinking back.
Your line: renounce, and enjoy. Today, when you notice yourself flinching from someone, stay one breath longer than you want to. Day two hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Isha verses 6 and 7 are often quoted by Hindu teachers, especially in the Vedanta traditions, as the root of seeing the one self in every being.

match.prompt: verses six to eight — tap the pairs.
pairs: and the self in all beings

myth: verse six says the cure for recoiling is to try harder to be nice
it's a way of seeing: all beings in the self, the self in all beings.
verse seven asks what sorrow there is for one who sees oneness
it's phrased as a question: what delusion, what sorrow?

fork.setup: you see the same self in yourself and in the stranger you'd rather avoid. what does verse six say happens?
options: you decide they are beneath you.
fork.reveal: the one who sees this way does not recoil from anything. the flinch loses its ground.

original.note: Sanskrit: ekatva, oneness; verse seven: for the one who sees oneness, what delusion, what sorrow?

trapdoor: what you thought: seeing everyone as one means everyone is the same.
what it means: seeing the same self in each being ends the recoil, not the differences.
what a scholar hears: 6 uses vijugupsate (to shrink in aversion); 7 asks tatra ko mohah kah shokah ekatvam anupashyatah.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 6–7 (all beings in the self; what sorrow for one who sees oneness)

notes: Verse 6 'na tato vijugupsate': some texts read 'vicikitsati' (doubts); check the recension.
Verse 8 list paraphrased (shukram, akayam, avranam, asnaviram, shuddham, apapaviddham, kavi, manishi, paribhuh, svayambhuh).
Gita 5.18 list (learned brahmin, cow, elephant, dog, dog-eater) paraphrased; check that the phrase 'the one who eats dogs' is acceptable wording for shvapaka.
